title: MB8-09476
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Pakistan, alleges that he fears the Molvi Nazir-ul-Haq, a local leader of Lashkar-e-Jhangvi (LeJ), an anti-Shia group. Upon his return from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) on XXXX XXXX, 2017, he was appointed XXXX of his local Imambargah and opened a XXXX XXXX office with a Christian friend. He left Pakistan on XXXX XXXX, 2017, to return to the UAE and arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017, to meet with organizations that could support his projects in Pakistan. He alleges that he began to fear for his life in mid-XXXX 2017 when his Christian friend began receiving threats over the telephone. His wife and father reportedly received anonymous threatening phone calls in XXXX 2017. In XXXX 2017, his wife received a pamphlet at home containing derogatory comments about the appellant, as well as another threatening call, and the XXXX office was allegedly attacked. Fearing for his life in Pakistan, he made a refugee protection claim.

The RPD found that the appellant's fear in Pakistan is not credible because he did not return to Pakistan on XXXX XXXX, 2017, before the alleged threats were issued in XXXX 2017. The panel also concluded that he was not at risk in Pakistan on the basis of his Shia faith.

The appellant alleges that the only reason the RPD found all of his evidence not to be credible is the fact that he did not leave Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017, as planned. He alleges that this ground is insufficient to reject all of the evidence that was before the panel.

The appeal is dismissed. The determinative issue is the appellant's credibility regarding his fear in Pakistan. The appellant testified that he did not return to Pakistan on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, because he already feared for his life, but then testified that he had nothing to fear at that time. He served as XXXX of the Imambargah and XXXX of the XXXX XXXX office for only two weeks before leaving Pakistan. He has not established that the Molvi or LeJ threatened or attacked him because he held those positions. His personal circumstances do not establish that he faces a serious possibility of persecution on the basis of his Shia faith. ANALYSIS Credibility The RPD did not err in its assessment of the appellant's credibility

In his memorandum, the appellant alleges that he gave lengthy testimony free of contradictions, inconsistencies and implausibilities. I do not accept this argument because he contradicted himself by claiming that he did not return to Pakistan on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, because of the threats against him, and that he did not hear about the threats until mid-XXXX 2017.

The appellant testified that he was scheduled to return to Pakistan on XXXX XXXX, 2017, because he was to be in Canada for only 13 days. At paragraph 21 of its reasons,1 the RPD describes the exchange that took place when it asked the appellant why he did not return to Pakistan on XXXX XXXX, 2017, and what information he received prior to that date in order for him to make this decision to stay in Canada. Having listened to the recording of the hearing, I confirm that the exchange as described by the RPD in its reasons is accurate. Furthermore, I add that the exchange with respect to this issue lasted from 1:12:24 to 1:25:41, which is more than ten minutes for this one and only issue. At least two of the long pauses that the appellant took before answering the questions lasted one minute. Finally, as noted by the RPD in its reasons, the appellant acknowledged that he had no information that would allow him to make a decision not to return to Pakistan because his life was at risk.

He alleges that the contradiction in relation to his return to Pakistan is the only reason given by the RPD for not believing that he is involved with the Imambargah and that he established a XXXX office before and after his departure from Pakistan. He alleges that the fact that he did not leave Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017, is insufficient to reject his entire story and evidence.

Having reviewed all of the evidence before me and listened to the tape recording of the hearing, I find that the RPD did not err in concluding that the appellant has not met the burden of establishing that there is a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be personally exposed to a risk of torture, a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon returning to his country. In this case, I find that the RPD's reasons were sufficient to justify rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

The appellant alleges that he feared for his life and therefore did not return to Pakistan. His own account2 establishes that the threats of concern began in XXXX 2017. In his memorandum, he alleges that an incident in the XXXX office on XXXX XXXX, 2017, was a reason for him to fear for his life and, therefore, to make the decision not to return to Pakistan on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. This is not what he said at the hearing. He testified that he did not yet have the information that prompted him to claim refugee protection in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017. I find that he sets out the reason for the incident of XXXX XXXX, 2017, in his appeal, in order to repair the credibility gap regarding his fear and to explain why he remained in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017.

The appellant claimed to be at risk because he was XXXX of his local Imambargah and because he opened a XXXX office with his Christian friend. The appellant left Pakistan on XXXX XXXX, 2017, and has been in Canada since XXXX XXXX, 2017.

The appellant testified that the XXXX office was opened on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. He testified that the office's only activity undertaken was the distribution by four to five people of pamphlets promoting XXXX XXXX in the community, and that this distribution took place on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. He confirmed that no other activities took place. He did not submit into evidence the pamphlet that was allegedly distributed to the community.

On a balance of probabilities, I find that the appellant has not established that he actually set up a XXXX office that would have attracted sufficient attention for him to be targeted for his activities and then threatened for this after he left Pakistan. The office was open for 13 days prior to his departure from Pakistan. It reportedly did only one activity: distributing an undetermined number of pamphlets in the community. No community events were held. He has not demonstrated that the alleged events took place, on a balance of probabilities, such that it may be concluded that he faces a serious possibility of persecution for that reason.

The appellant alleges that his risk is also related to his role as XXXX of the Imambargah, a position he obtained on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. He left Pakistan on XXXX XXXX, 2017, and never returned. He testified that, as XXXX, he was responsible for XXXX XXXX XXXX of the Imambargah, including the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. I do not believe that the appellant had the time to take over the XXXX of the Imambargah in a way that would have drawn the attention of the Molvi Nazir-l-Haq and the LeJ to the point where the group threatened his life. His testimony establishes that, concretely, in carrying out his tasks, he XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He confirmed that he did nothing other than XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The appellant would have held the role for 13 days and would not have had time to build a profile of high enough visibility to attract this threatening attention as XXXX of the Imambargah, on the balance of probabilities.

He alleges that his father was the XXXX of the Imambargah for 20 years and that his family is known in the community. However, the evidence on the record does not indicate that his father was threatened for this reason. I do not believe that after 13 days of XXXX and after two months of absence (the threats allegedly started in mid-XXXX 2017) the appellant would be targeted by the Molvi and the LeJ for this reason. The RPD did not err in giving little probative value to the evidence corroborating his allegations

The appellant alleges that the RPD did not give any probative value to the numerous documents corroborating his allegations because the panel had already concluded that the threats were not credible. The RPD gave little probative value to his corroborating evidence because he could not establish a fear that he had not credibly established.

The appellant testified that he feared nothing in XXXX 2017, while his wife's affidavit3 states that he feared for his life and has remained in Canada since XXXX 2017 because his life was threatened by the Molvi. His wife's affidavit contradicts his testimony, so I do not find her testimony to be credible in relation to the testimony in his affidavit.

His father's affidavit and the letters from his lawyer and the local imam cannot rectify the appellant's lack of credibility with respect to his fear. All three pieces of evidence refer to testimony given by the appellant. The appellant's testimony is not credible, and the credibility of this evidence, all of which was provided after XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, is therefore undermined. For this reason, like the RPD, I find that these documents in evidence have little probative value.

Although the XXXX office was allegedly attacked in XXXX 2017, the appellant has not established that he is at risk for this reason because he was not in Pakistan; the reason he remained in Canada is not related to this alleged attack. The fact that he remained in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017, without any of these alleged incidents between XXXX and XXXX 2017 having occurred undermines the credibility of his fear, and makes the corroborating evidence on this issue suspect.

The appellant filed a newspaper article published on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. The content of the article refers to details of his travels, including the fact that he is currently abroad and has returned to Pakistan after several years abroad. When asked how the newspaper obtained this information, he replied that he did not know and then adjusted his testimony to state that his Christian friend gave them the information. When asked how he obtained the article and who informed him of the attack on the office, he offered confused testimony about when he knew the office was attacked and who informed him of the attack.4 His testimony and the fact that the content includes details that would be difficult to obtain without the appellant's cooperation leads me to conclude that the item is fraudulent and was designed to support his claim for refugee protection on a balance of probabilities.

With respect to his corroborating evidence, I note that the appellant alleges that he received the originals of this evidence after the RPD decision, but did not file them as evidence before the RAD. He leaves it to the RAD to make the request to see the original documents if necessary. However, he does not explain why he could not file the documents with the RPD since the RPD gave him additional time after the hearing to file them.5 This undermines his credibility.

I find that if the appellant were credible with respect to his fear in Pakistan: a. He would not have responded that he remained in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017, when he was scheduled to leave, and that he had nothing to fear according to his testimony and account. b. He would have had a more concrete role with a concrete contribution within the Imambargah and the XXXX XXXX office, demonstrating that he was threatened for these reasons. c. Given that he has been in Canada since XXXX XXXX, 2017, and that the hearing was held more than a year later, he would have provided the original versions of his corroborating evidence before the day of the RPD hearing, thus within the time limit prescribed by the regulations.6 d. He would have provided the original versions of his corroborating evidence by April 9, 2018, within the extension of time granted by the RPD.
For all these reasons, I find that the appellant is not credible with respect to his fear in Pakistan. Residual profile

Noting that the need for international protection for Shiites depends on their personal circumstances,7 and after analysis, the RPD found that the appellant did not face a serious possibility of persecution in Pakistan because of his Shia faith.

The appellant argues that if his personal circumstances had been reasonably analyzed, the documentary evidence would have supported his fear. He alleges that he did not claim refugee protection until January 2017 because his life was not in danger at that time. He alleges that his life has been in danger since 2017 because he took over the XXXX of his Imambargah.

Having already concluded that he did not demonstrate that he is at risk because he took over the XXXX of the Imambargah and that he did not show that his father was at risk for this reason after 20 years of XXXX and influence within his Shiite community, I do not accept this argument.
As for his role as XXXX of the Imambargah, I have already concluded that his contribution was not significant enough to attract the attention and the alleged threats.

According to the documentary evidence, the Shia are about 10% to 15% of Pakistan's population and have enjoyed significant influence in Pakistani society.8 In addition, according to this evidence, it is the Shia of Hazara ethnicity, who are predominantly concentrated in Quetta in the province of Balochistan, who may be at risk due to their personal circumstances.9 The city of Quetta and the province of Balochistan are recognized as places affected by terrorism.10

The appellant alleges discrimination on the basis of his Shia status, in particular because his employment opportunities as a XXXX have been restricted. The documentary evidence indicates that Shia people may be discriminated against in Pakistan.11 Taking into account that his family has a significant presence in his community and the fact that he has not indicated any other elements of discrimination suffered, the cumulative experience of his family does not lead to the conclusion that this discrimination meets the threshold for a finding of persecution.

Given the documentary evidence of the risk to Shiites in Pakistan, and considering the low profile he would have built up during his 13 days as Imambargah XXXX before leaving Pakistan, I am of the opinion that he does not face a serious possibility of persecution on account of his Shia faith and his role as XXXX of the Imambargah, nor would he personally face a risk of torture, a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon returning to his country, on a balance of probabilities.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the impugned decision that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
